title: Counterfeit Reasons
coreMove: Treat the stated reason as a press release and inspect what decision it was written to justify.
sourcePressure: The source argues that people fabricate counterfeit reasons after the fact, with split-brain and confabulation evidence supporting the press-secretary model of the ego.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer turns counterfeit reasons into ordinary excuses and misses post-hoc confabulation.

sourceAnchors.name: split-brain and confabulation evidence
sourceAnchors.detail: The source says split-brain and confabulation evidence support the claim that minds generate reasons after the fact.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The reason can arrive cleanly after the choice, like a caption pasted under a photograph.

sourceAnchors.name: ego as press secretary
sourceAnchors.detail: The source says the ego behaves more like a press secretary than a central executive.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The press secretary does not run the government; it explains the government after the door closes.

sourceAnchors.name: strategic ignorance about motives
sourceAnchors.detail: The source says people can be strategically ignorant about motives.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A person can avoid knowing the motive that would make the public story harder to sell.

hook: the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: do not open with a confession that everyone has hidden motives
the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: avoid the tidy X is not really Y shell
counterintuition: the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: no blanket cynicism that turns all public reasons into lies
the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: avoid a simple pure-versus-fake contrast
tryThisNow: the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: no reusable notice your motives prompt
examples: the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: no office meeting with a whiteboard as the default scene
the-elephant-in-the-brain-ch06: no coffee shop conversation as the default social proof

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.audience: a juror explaining a favorite design after the vote
exampleSpecs.stakes: the official reason may be a caption added after faction preference won
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Thomas compares the juror's praise to the vote order and notices the environmental language appeared only after Margaux's favored firm led.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Scale models cast long shadows across the jury table.

exampleSpecs.audience: a product manager sorting real constraints from invented rationale
exampleSpecs.stakes: a team may rationalize a feature because an executive already wanted it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "Customers asked for simplicity," Mikkel says, and Emily opens the support logs to test whether simplicity existed before the decision.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Customers asked for simplicity," Mikkel says as the roadmap card moves columns.

exampleSpecs.audience: a sibling defending an unequal keepsake split
exampleSpecs.stakes: the spoken fairness rule may appear after desire has already chosen
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Aman sets the watch, quilt, and appraisal sheet on separate placemats and asks which fairness rule existed before anyone picked an object.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The watch ticks loudly on a placemat beside the folded quilt.

exampleSpecs.audience: a researcher explaining why one paper deserves discussion
exampleSpecs.stakes: status alignment may be hidden behind methods language
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What reason survives after the famous author's name is blacked out?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What reason survives when the author line is hidden under black tape?

exampleSpecs.audience: a reviewer defending a downtown project over a boring repair
exampleSpecs.stakes: post-hoc reasons can make prestige preference sound civic-minded
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You ask Chiara to score blind project descriptions before seeing neighborhood names, then compare which reasons appear only after downtown becomes visible.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You watch the downtown name change the temperature of the room.

exampleSpecs.audience: an owner justifying an expensive redesign as readability
exampleSpecs.stakes: a taste for prestige may be disguised as customer clarity
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Margaux until the invoice arrived to admit the readability reason never mentioned the gold foil until after she saw it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Margaux until the printer's invoice to reread her own brief.

skillTargets: distinguish central-executive stories from press-secretary stories
test a stated reason against pre-decision evidence

tryThisNowSpec: Take one decision already made. Before defending it, write what evidence would have changed your mind before the choice became yours.
